summary: Proposes an architecture, called MALLOC, for allocating multicast addresses on the Internet. It describes layers of allocation, from clients to servers to inter-domain mechanisms. It was later marked historic. It was replaced by RFC 6308.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people want to use group-chat addresses without picking the same one. This proposes a system of hand-outs so each group gets its own.

questions: how does multicast address allocation work
what are the three layers of malloc
subtitle: A three-layer architecture for handing out multicast addresses without collisions.

tldr.problem: Many applications want multicast addresses, but addresses must be unique within their scope to avoid collisions. Manual allocation does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: MALLOC proposes a three-layer architecture: clients request addresses from local servers (Layer 1), servers coordinate with peers to avoid reuse (Layer 2), and domain coordinators share address ranges across the Internet (Layer 3).
tldr.outcome: The architecture was marked historic and replaced by RFC 6308, which supersedes it.

facts.label: Address lifetime
facts.value: Can range from temporary to permanent

today: RFC 2908 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 6308, which updates the multicast address allocation architecture.

sections.title: The Multicast Address Problem
sections.content:
Multicast allows one sender to reach many receivers at once by using a single group address. But unlike a unicast address that identifies one computer, a multicast address can mean different things in different places. Two applications could both use the same multicast address (say, 239.1.2.3) without knowing about each other, causing traffic from one to reach the other's receivers.

The RFC identifies two dimensions that limit address use: lifetime (when an address is valid) and scope (where it is valid, such as within a building, a domain, or globally). An allocation system must ensure addresses do not collide within their scope and lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: Group addresses need to be unique, or messages get mixed up. The system needs to hand them out to keep everyone's chats separate.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC outlines four key properties an allocation system must have:

Robustness: An application asking for an address should get one, even if the network is partially broken.

Timeliness: Allocation should happen within seconds, not hours.

Low collision probability: When scarce, the system should minimize collisions rather than guarantee none, because guarantees force fragmentation of the address space that makes allocation less efficient.

Address space efficiency: When addresses are hard to get, waste should be minimized. The RFC prioritizes availability and good use of space over absolute guarantees of no collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should give out addresses quickly, work when parts of the network are broken, avoid mixing up addresses as much as possible, and not waste the available addresses.

sections.title: The Three-Layer Architecture
sections.content:
MALLOC has three layers, each independent and replaceable:

Layer 1 (Host-Server): A client (the application) asks a Multicast Address Allocation Server (MAAS) for an address. This can use protocols like MADCAP or even HTTP. Once the server grants an address with a lifetime, the server promises not to reuse that address within its scope during that time.

Layer 2 (Intra-Domain): Multiple servers within a domain (an administrative region) coordinate to avoid allocating the same address. They may partition the address space in advance, or use a protocol like AAP to announce and verify allocations. An administrator called a Prefix Coordinator manages address ranges for the domain.

Layer 3 (Inter-Domain): Prefix Coordinators in different domains coordinate to divvy up large address spaces. Protocols like MASC allow routers to claim and manage address ranges across the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Layer 1 is like asking your local librarian for a book number. Layer 2 is the librarians in your building checking with each other. Layer 3 is different cities' library systems sharing which numbers they control.

sections.title: Three Ways to Allocate Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC defines three types of allocation:

Static allocation: IANA reserves well-known addresses for specific protocols (like 224.0.1.1 for Network Time Protocol). These have a permanent lifetime and are valid everywhere.

Scope-relative allocation: RFC 2365 reserves the top 256 addresses in each scope for offsets that are the same in every scope. Infrastructure protocols (like multicast zone announcements) use these.

Dynamic allocation: The most common case. A client requests an address for a session with a specific lifetime. The server allocates it, and when the lifetime expires, the client should request a new address or ask for an extension. This allows the system to recycle addresses and keep the address space packed efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses are permanent and famous, some are the same in every scope, and most are rented for a while and returned.

sections.title: Scopes and Allocation Domains
sections.content:
Administrative scoping divides the network into regions, each with its own multicast address ranges. Small scopes (like a building) are handled entirely within that scope using Layer 2 coordination. Large scopes (like the global scope) are split into allocation domains aligned with Autonomous System (AS) boundaries when possible.

To reduce fragmentation, the RFC defines the Allocation Scope—a special administrative scope used just for coordination. In IPv4, this is 239.251.0.0/16; in IPv6, it is scope value 6. Every domain participates in the Allocation Scope to claim ranges for large scopes.
sections.plainLanguage: Big spaces are divided into manageable regions so servers can each handle their part. A special region is used just for the servers to talk to each other.
